job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Nikhil Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a master's in machine learning at Kawagoe Institute, and I share a flat with two other students near campus. A normal day starts with an hour of code with an AI assistant open next to me, then lab meetings, then my own side project: a small app that helps local shops answer customer messages. I graduated top of my computer science class, with internships at a payments start-up and at a university research lab. I freelance a bit on weekends for about 300 a month. I use AI tools all day, and I'm the person my friends ask when they're stuck on a prompt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, that matches what I see anyway. The tools are useful but they hit a ceiling, and people who thought they'd replace programmers were overselling. I'd keep posting about my side project and say good engineers still matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's a bit boring, to be honest. I've bet a lot on the idea that this stuff matters, and a plateau means a normal career and fewer big opportunities. I'd still be okay, because my skills are strong whichever way it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, take the best offer from the payments start-up where I interned, and keep my weekend freelance work. I'd put 200 a month into an index fund. And I'd keep building the shop-messaging app, because even a plateau leaves room for small useful tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly restless, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's a bit boring. Boring how?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like being near something that changes fast. A plateau means I'd be doing standard backend work for ten years. That's a fine life, I just don't hear it calling me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do if the start-up doesn't make you an offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have three other places that said they'd talk after graduation, and my old lab supervisor, Dr Mehta, would take me as a research assistant. I'm not nervous about that part.

say: The tools are **useful** but they hit a ceiling, and the hype was overdone.
think: A plateau means a **normal career**, which is fine but a little dull.
My skills are strong whichever way it goes, so my **job search** feels safe.
do: Finish the master's and take the best offer from the **payments start-up**.
Put **200 a month** into an index fund.
Keep building my shop-messaging **app** on weekends.
S0.quote: I like being near something that changes fast. A plateau means I'd be doing standard backend work for ten years.
fieldNote: Nikhil's calm is real: he has offers in the **pipeline** and skills that sell either way.
His only complaint is that a plateau feels **boring** for someone who bet on change.

steps.text: Accept the best offer from the payments start-up after graduating
Put 200 a month into an index fund
Keep freelancing on weekends for about 300 a month
Finish the master's thesis on schedule

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the world I'm betting on. I'd say it's exciting and that people should start using the tools now, instead of arguing about them. I'd also say companies must retrain, not just cut, because I've seen both approaches at my internships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the junior coding role changes quickly, and that's me. But I'm the one who can build with these tools, so I'm on the right side of this for a few years. Where I'd worry is for friends who don't use them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd turn my app into a proper small business: sign up ten local shops at 20 a month each and add an AI helper for their bookings. I'd take a part-time job as an AI engineer while finishing the master's. And I'd run a free workshop for my friends who are behind on the tools, because I'd rather they not be left out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, with a bit of guilt, because I'm ahead and many friends aren't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd start a business at the same time as a master's. How do you manage that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cut sleep and weekends, which isn't healthy. I'd set a hard rule: if the shops don't hit 2,000 a month by next summer, I stop and take the full-time job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you worry about among your friends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Kaito (his friend from the flat) is brilliant at maths but refuses to touch the tools. I keep telling him to try for one week.

say: This is **exciting**, and people should start using the tools now instead of arguing.
Companies must **retrain** their people, not just cut them.
think: The junior coding role changes **fast**, but I can build with the tools.
I worry more about **friends** who don't use them.
do: Sign up **ten local shops** at 20 a month for my app.
Take a part-time **AI engineer** job during the master's.
Run a free **workshop** on the tools for friends.
feel: **Excited**, with a bit of guilt because I'm ahead of friends.
S1.quote: I'd set a hard rule: if the shops don't hit 2,000 a month by next summer, I stop and take the full-time job.
fieldNote: Nikhil sees this card as an **opportunity** and has a concrete, time-limited plan with a stop rule.
His worry is about **friends** like Kaito who refuse the tools, not about himself.

steps.text: Sign up ten local shops at 20 a month for the app
Add an AI booking helper to the shop app
Take a part-time AI engineer job during the master's
Run a free workshop on AI tools for friends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the biggest thing in history and we're not ready. I'd post a long thread about demanding public oversight, a safety testing regime and some form of income support. Honestly, I'd also say that I'm excited, and I'd get told off for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, even I'm scared. I'm good now, but if AI does almost any thinking job better and cheaper, my edge is gone and so is the start-up that hires me. My 300 a month freelance work and my little app are exactly what an AGI would do for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending, which is easy for me, and save every cent, about 900 a month if I can get a full-time job. I'd call the start-up and see if I can start immediately, rather than wait for the master's to finish. I'd also join an AI safety group and lobby my representative, because policy matters more than my code at that point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm in the most exposed field with the most useful skills, which is a strange feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd drop the master's for a job. Isn't that a big step?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but a degree that takes two years to finish is a slow bet in a fast game. I'd rather take a salary and some savings, and my parents could lend me about 3,000 if needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you feel about your own part in this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit complicated. I've helped train and test these systems at the lab, so I feel responsible and also awed. I think people like me should be vocal about oversight.

say: This is the **biggest thing** in history and we're not ready.
We need public **oversight**, safety testing and income support.
think: Even with my skills, my **edge** could be gone and so could the start-up.
My freelance work and app are what **AGI** would do for free.
do: Ask the start-up to take me on **immediately**.
Save about **900 a month** from a full-time salary.
Join an AI **safety group** and lobby my representative.
feel: **Anxious**, because I'm in the most exposed field.
S2.quote: I'm in the most exposed field with the most useful skills, which is a strange feeling.
fieldNote: Nikhil is the **best prepared** person for this card and is still anxious, which shows how fast two years feels.
He feels some **responsibility**, because he has worked on the systems.

steps.text: Ask the payments start-up to hire me now, before graduation
Save about 900 a month from the first salary
Lobby my representative for AI safety testing and oversight
Join a student AI safety group and attend its meetings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build something sensible if we start now. I'd say we need retraining, public testing of the systems and a plan for who gets the benefits. Online I'd argue for open debate, not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm uneasy, but I'd have time to build skills and maybe my own business. By 2031 I'd be 29 with years of experience, savings, and perhaps a company with a few employees. That's a good place to meet AGI from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the start-up job and work there for two years while growing my own product on the side. I'd invest about 400 a month and also pick up a robotics side project, since hands-on work is where the next three years of change are coming. I'd keep teaching friends the tools, because networks matter when everything's shifting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but ready. This is the speed I could keep up with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why robotics?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in a world where thinking is cheap, the interesting work is where software meets the physical world. I'd want to be on that side before everyone else gets there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your own company doesn't work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm still a well-paid engineer with a record. I have enough fallback to try, and that's the point of five years.

say: Five years is enough to build something **sensible** if we start now.
We need retraining, public **testing** and a plan for who gets the benefits.
think: I'd have time to build **skills** and maybe a small company.
By 2031 I'd be a **well-paid** engineer with savings.
do: Work at the start-up for **two years** while building my own product.
S3.quote: In a world where thinking is cheap, the interesting work is where software meets the physical world.
fieldNote: Nikhil's best answer here is about **robotics**, which shows him looking for the next gap, not defending the last one.
Five years gives him room to try a **company** with a fallback.

steps.text: Work at the start-up for two years and learn how it runs
Grow my shop-messaging product on the side into a small company
Invest 400 a month in an index fund
Start a robotics control project with the university lab

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and we should use it to build good rules, fair taxes and strong retraining. I'd also say that anyone who's under 30 now should learn to build with these tools, not just use them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, calm. By 2036 I'd be 34. I could have built a company, sold it or failed at it, and be fine. I'd still worry about people less equipped than me, but I'd have time and money to help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, work in industry, and start a company at some point in the next five years. I'd buy a small flat, with a loan I can handle, and put steady money into an index fund. And I'd keep volunteering to teach coding, because it's good for me too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and quite happy, which is rare for me when I think about the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you less calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If everyone just assumed ten years means nothing needs doing. I've seen how fast the field moves, and ten years can pass in a blink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there something in your plan you'd be embarrassed to say online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I want to be rich enough to not worry. It sounds shallow, but being freelance on 300 a month taught me what worry feels like.

say: Ten years is a **gift**, so we should build rules and fair taxes now.
People under 30 should learn to **build** with the tools.
think: By 2036 I'd be 34 and **fine** whether a company works or fails.
I'd still worry about people **less equipped** than me.
do: Finish the master's and work in **industry**.
Buy a small **flat** with a loan I can handle.
feel: **Calm** and quite happy, which is rare when I think about the future.
S4.quote: I want to be rich enough to not worry. It sounds shallow, but being freelance on 300 a month taught me what worry feels like.
fieldNote: Nikhil is **calm** because ten years lets him try, fail and recover.
His private motive is **security**, which differs from his public talk about rules and fairness.

steps.text: Finish the master's and work in industry for two years
Start my own company within five years
Put steady money into an index fund every month
Buy a small flat with a loan I can handle

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, even though I'm the best placed for it. Two years leaves no room to try and fail. What would help is public safety testing, income support for people who can't keep up, and open access to the tools so it's not just a few firms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that being good with the tools doesn't make me safe, and I feel guilty about how many of my friends aren't. I'd like to build something that helps them, not just me.

headlineQuote: Being good with the tools doesn't make me safe, and I feel guilty about how many of my friends aren't.
portrait: Nikhil is a 24-year-old **computer science** graduate doing a master's in machine learning, using AI tools every day.
He freelances for about 300 a month and is building a small **app** for local shops.
He leans progressive, wants public oversight and **safety testing**, and feels guilty about friends who lag.
His mood is calm in most cases, rising to **anxious** at two years because his own field is most exposed.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years leaves no room to try and fail.
whatWouldHelp: Public safety testing, **income support** and open access to the tools.
